title: Leaders Worthy of God’s Household
summary: Paul sets out the character required of overseers and deacons, then grounds church order in God’s household and the confessed mystery of Christ.
historicalContext: Paul had left Timothy at Ephesus to restrain teachers who were spreading speculative myths and misusing the law (1:3-7). The believers of the city met in households under elders whom Paul had once warned that wolves would arise from among their own number (Acts 20:29-30). That warning was already being fulfilled: Hymenaeus and Alexander had made shipwreck of the faith (1:20), and the disorder addressed in chapter 2 suggests that false teaching had unsettled both worship and home life. The choice of leaders was therefore urgent. Ephesus was a proud civic center, home to the great temple of Artemis and to a populace quick to turn on a new movement (Acts 19:23-41). Lists of virtues expected of generals, magistrates, and heads of households circulated widely in that culture. Paul’s qualifications overlap with them at points, yet they are shaped throughout by teaching, faith, conscience, and the gospel of Christ.
literaryContext: Chapter 3 continues the instructions for congregational life that began in 2:1. After prayer and the conduct of men and women in worship, Paul turns to those who lead: overseers (3:1-7) and deacons (3:8-13), with a brief word about women connected to diaconal service (3:11). The two lists share much, but only the overseer must be “apt to teach” and “take care of the church of God.” Verses 14-16 pause to state the purpose of the letter: Timothy is to know how people ought to conduct themselves in God’s household, the church that upholds the truth. The chapter then rises into a confession of Christ whose six lines move from incarnation to exaltation. That hymn anchors church order in the person of Christ and prepares for the warning about departure from the faith in 4:1-5.
themes: Character as the foundation of leadership
The home as the proving ground for oversight
Leadership as service rather than status
The church as God’s household upholding the truth
The incarnate and exalted Christ at the center

outline.title: Qualifications for Overseers
outline.summary: Paul commends the desire for oversight and lists the moral, domestic, and spiritual qualities that must mark those who care for the church of God.

outline.title: Deacons Proved and Found Blameless
outline.summary: Deacons must be serious, honest in speech, free from indulgence and greed, settled in the faith with a clean conscience, and tested before serving.

outline.title: Women, Households, and the Reward of Service
outline.summary: Women connected with diaconal service must be trustworthy, deacons must lead faithful homes, and those who serve well gain standing and confidence in Christ.

outline.title: The Household of the Living God
outline.summary: Paul explains that he writes so that conduct in God’s household, the church that upholds the truth, may be rightly ordered.

outline.title: The Great Mystery of Godliness
outline.summary: An early confession celebrates Christ manifested in flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, proclaimed among the nations, and received up into glory.

verses.bibleText: This is a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“This is a true saying” renders the same formula that introduced 1:15, the second of the letter’s trustworthy sayings. Whether it looks back to the closing words about salvation in 2:15 or forward to the statement about oversight has long been debated. The forward reading fits best, since a compact, proverb-like sentence follows at once and the next verses unfold it. Either way, Paul places a solemn endorsement on what he says. Leadership among God’s people deserves the same seriousness he gave to the gospel itself.

“The office of a bishop” translates a single Greek word for oversight. In the apostolic churches the overseer was the same person called an elder, as Acts 20:17 and 28 and Titus 1:5 and 7 show by using both titles for one group. The later figure of a single bishop presiding over many congregations belongs to a subsequent century. At Ephesus a body of elders cared for believers meeting in homes, and the false teaching of chapter 1 had apparently found a voice among some who claimed to teach. Timothy needed to know what kind of men could be trusted with that charge.

Paul treats the aspiration favorably. Two verbs of desire appear. The first pictures reaching out toward something; the second expresses strong longing. Neither carries reproach. To want to shepherd God’s people is a worthy desire when the thing desired is “a good work”—labor, service, the weight of caring for souls. The phrase turns attention away from title and position toward the task.

That emphasis needs restating in every generation. A congregation flourishes when those drawn to leadership want to serve more than to be seen, and the list that follows will test the desire: whoever longs for oversight must accept having his character examined. Christ, “the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls,” is the pattern of an overseer who came to give himself for the flock.

wordNotes.term: ἐπισκοπή (episkopē) — the office of a bishop
wordNotes.explanation: The noun denotes oversight, the responsibility of watching over and caring for others. In the New Testament the overseer (episkopos) and the elder (presbyteros) name the same local leader from two angles: one describes the task, the other the maturity expected. The word does not yet carry the later sense of a diocesan bishop.

The verb means to stretch out toward or aspire to something. Here it carries no hint of selfish ambition; Paul calls the aspiration good because its object is a good work. The same verb describes the patriarchs reaching toward a better, heavenly country.

verses.bibleText: A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Must” translates a word of necessity: these qualities belong to the nature of the office. The first requirement gathers up the rest. The overseer is to be “blameless,” one against whom no accusation can justly be fastened. Paul is not demanding sinless perfection, which would disqualify every candidate, but a life whose settled public pattern offers no handle for reproach. Most items in the list are ordinary Christian virtues. What makes them weighty is that they are required, observed, and tested before anyone receives responsibility. Gifts, eloquence, and administrative skill are not mentioned first. Character is.

“The husband of one wife” is literally “a one-woman man.” It has been read as requiring marriage, as forbidding a second marriage after a spouse dies, as excluding anyone divorced, or as demanding monogamy and marital faithfulness. The first reading is unlikely. Paul himself was unmarried and commended singleness for undistracted service (1 Corinthians 7:7-8, 32-35); the phrase assumes the common situation of a married man without making marriage a condition. Scripture nowhere treats a widower’s remarriage as a moral failure (Romans 7:2-3; 1 Corinthians 7:39). The wording most naturally requires a man whose marital and sexual life is wholly faithful—devoted to one woman, with no rival attachments—in a culture that tolerated concubines, casual infidelity, and in some communities polygamy. It also rules out any law of compulsory celibacy, a teaching 4:3 will expose as error. Questions arising from past divorce call for pastoral judgment shaped by Christ’s words in Matthew 19:9, with the controlling concern that the man’s present home commend the gospel.

The next three terms describe an ordered mind. “Vigilant” renders a word associated with sobriety and clear-headedness, freedom from whatever dulls judgment. “Sober” means sound-minded and self-controlled. “Of good behaviour” describes an orderly, well-arranged life, using the root that described modest dress in 2:9. Such men stay steady when a church is agitated by novelty or controversy.

“Given to hospitality” mattered greatly when traveling believers relied on Christian homes and congregations gathered in houses; the overseer keeps an open door. “Apt to teach” is the one item that names a skill. He must be able to explain and apply sound doctrine and, as Titus 1:9 adds, answer those who contradict it. At Ephesus, where some wanted “to be teachers of the law” without understanding it (1:7), this capacity was essential. Ability to teach grows out of being taught, and the man who instructs others must remain a learner of the Word himself.

wordNotes.explanation: The adjective describes someone who cannot be laid hold of by an accuser, whose conduct gives no fair occasion for censure. It speaks of reputation that is deserved, not merely a polished image. Paul applies the same standard to widows enrolled for support and to Timothy’s own keeping of the charge.

wordNotes.term: μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα (mias gynaikos andra) — the husband of one wife
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “a man of one woman,” the phrase stresses exclusive marital faithfulness. The parallel “wife of one man” for enrolled widows in 5:9 shows that the expression describes fidelity of character. It does not make marriage a requirement for office, and Scripture elsewhere leaves a widowed believer free to marry again in the Lord.

verses.bibleText: Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Verse 3 turns largely to what the overseer must not be, and its negatives cluster around two dangers: loss of self-control and love of gain. “Not given to wine” describes one who does not sit long beside wine or come under its power. In a world where drinking was woven into banquets, trade-guild meals, and household life, a leader must not be known as one who indulges. Scripture’s wider warnings against intoxicating drink (Proverbs 20:1; 23:29-32) and its call to keep body and mind fit for God (1 Corinthians 6:19-20) point to a clear judgment: the shepherd should be a model of temperance, keeping his mind unclouded for the work entrusted to him.

“No striker” refers to a man quick with his fists; “not a brawler” to one who is quarrelsome and enjoys a fight. Between them stands the single positive word, “patient,” better rendered gentle or reasonable. It describes a considerate forbearance that yields wherever principle allows. Paul uses the related noun of “the meekness and gentleness of Christ.” Oversight in a church troubled by contentious teachers who doted on “strifes of words” (6:4) demanded men who could stand firm without becoming combative.

“Not covetous” is literally “not a lover of silver.” The KJV’s “not greedy of filthy lucre” is absent from the oldest manuscripts at this point and appears to have been carried over from verse 8 and Titus 1:7; its meaning is already contained in “not covetous.” The false teachers supposed “that gain is godliness” (6:5), and Judas showed how love of money can corrupt even an apostle’s place. A shepherd whose heart is set on money will eventually use the flock for profit. One who has learned contentment can be trusted with its resources and its confidence.

wordNotes.explanation: The word describes gentleness, reasonableness, and a readiness to yield rather than insist on one’s rights. It belongs to the wisdom from above and marks the kind of forbearance believers are to show toward all people. In leaders it is the opposite of the striker and the brawler named on either side of it.

Literally “not a lover of silver.” The term excludes a heart attached to money rather than the honest handling of it. Hebrews uses the same word for the contentment that rests on God’s promise never to forsake his people.

verses.bibleText: One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul moves from personal disposition to the household. “One that ruleth well his own house” uses a verb meaning to stand before or preside, with the added sense of caring leadership. The same verb describes elders who “rule well” in 5:17 and those who are “over you in the Lord” in 1 Thessalonians 5:12. A first-century household was larger than a modern family, often including relatives and servants as well as children, and how a man ordered that circle was visible to the whole community.

“Having his children in subjection with all gravity” can be read two ways. The gravity may describe the children’s respectful conduct, or it may describe the father’s dignified manner in guiding them. The two belong together. A harsh father may produce outward compliance, and a careless one produces disorder. Paul commends a home where children are led with dignity and respond with respect—order without tyranny. Ephesians 6:4 adds the warning that fathers must not provoke their children to wrath.

The requirement concerns the ordinary course of a home, not a guarantee that every child will choose faith. Eli’s failure to restrain his sons is the sobering example: a priest who indulged his household lost his ministry. What Paul has in view is the father’s faithful oversight while children remain under his care. Where that is plainly lacking, the man’s readiness for wider oversight is rightly in question.

wordNotes.explanation: The participle comes from a verb meaning to stand at the head of, to lead or manage. In Paul it combines authority with care, describing those who lead diligently and labor among the believers. It recurs for elders who rule well, linking leadership at home with leadership in the church.

wordNotes.term: μετὰ πάσης σεμνότητος (meta pasēs semnotētos) — with all gravity
wordNotes.explanation: The noun denotes dignity, seriousness, and a bearing that earns respect. Earlier in the letter it describes the godly and dignified life believers seek through prayer for those in authority. Here it marks a household ordered with respect rather than mere compulsion.

verses.bibleText: (For if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?)

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The parenthesis supplies Paul’s reasoning. If a man does not know how to lead his own household, how will he care for the church of God? The argument moves from the smaller sphere to the larger. The home is a proving ground, and faithfulness in little reveals readiness for more. Patient instruction, fair discipline, and steady provision are tested first where no one is watching for public approval.

The verb changes between the two halves. For the home Paul says “rule”; for the church he says “take care of.” The same word describes the Samaritan’s care for the wounded traveler and his instruction to the innkeeper. Oversight of God’s people is attentive, tender concern for their welfare. The church also belongs to Another: it is “the church of God,” which he purchased with his own blood. The overseer is a steward in someone else’s house, accountable to its Owner for every member.

The verse prepares for 3:15, where the church is called “the house of God.” The household image runs through the letter. Timothy is to treat older men as fathers and younger women as sisters (5:1-2), and believers are to provide for their own relatives (5:8). A congregation is a family, and its leaders must know how to lead a family.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to look after or attend to the needs of someone. It is used of the Samaritan who cared for the wounded man and arranged for his continuing care. Paul chooses it to show that oversight in God’s church is personal and protective, not merely administrative.

verses.bibleText: Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Not a novice” translates a word meaning “newly planted,” used figuratively for a recent convert. Scripture sets no minimum age for church leaders—Timothy himself was young (4:12)—but it does require spiritual maturity proven over time. By this point the Ephesian church had existed for more than a decade, long enough to have tested members available. The parallel list in Titus omits this requirement, perhaps because the congregations on Crete were newer.

The danger is pride. “Lifted up with pride” renders a word that pictures being wrapped in smoke, beclouded, puffed up. Sudden elevation can intoxicate a believer who has not yet learned the depth of his own weakness. Responsibility granted too quickly feeds the illusion that he has arrived, and conceit blurs judgment at the very moment clear sight is most needed.

“The condemnation of the devil” most naturally means the judgment that fell on the devil because of his pride. Scripture traces the beginning of evil to a created being who exalted himself against God (Isaiah 14:12-15; Ezekiel 28:12-17). Lucifer, made perfect, was not content with his place and coveted honor that belongs to God alone. His fall opened a controversy that runs through all human history. A church leader who grows proud repeats that first rebellion in miniature and falls under the same verdict. Some take the phrase as the condemnation brought by the devil as accuser (Revelation 12:10), but judgment belongs to God, and the link with pride favors the first sense.

Christ’s way runs in the opposite direction. He “made himself of no reputation,” and God highly exalted him after he humbled himself. The leader the church needs has learned that lesson by experience: “God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.”

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “newly planted,” the word is the source of “neophyte.” Paul uses a gardening picture for one only recently set into the life of the church, whose roots have not yet gone down. The concern is maturity, not age, as the call for roots and growth elsewhere shows.

The verb is connected with smoke or mist and, in the passive, means to be puffed up or blinded by conceit. Paul uses it again for the proud false teacher who knows nothing and for those in the last days who are “highminded.” Pride is pictured as a fog that clouds perception.

verses.bibleText: Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Moreover he must” repeats the language of necessity. The overseer’s reputation is now viewed from outside the church. “A good report of them which are without” means that unbelievers in the community—neighbors, trading partners, civic acquaintances—should be able to say that this man is honest, fair, and decent. Outsiders do not choose the church’s leaders, yet their testimony about a man’s conduct carries weight. A pagan neighbor could not judge Christian doctrine, but he could recognize a cheat or a hypocrite.

This concern runs through the Pastoral letters. Believers are to live so that “the name of God and his doctrine be not blasphemed” (6:1) and so that the adversary has no occasion to speak reproachfully (5:14; Titus 2:5, 8). The church at Ephesus lived under suspicion, and the riot of Acts 19 had shown how quickly hostility could flare. A leader with a stained name in the city would hand opponents a ready weapon.

“Lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil” joins disgrace with danger. A snare is set where it is not seen. The devil uses public scandal to discredit the gospel, and he uses a leader’s embarrassment to push him toward defensiveness, concealment, and further sin. Second Timothy speaks of those caught in that snare who may yet be recovered through repentance. The safeguard is integrity that keeps the same shape in the marketplace as at the Lord’s table. The conflict between Christ and Satan concerns whether God’s people display his character before a watching world as well as what they believe.

wordNotes.term: μαρτυρίαν καλὴν (martyrian kalēn) — a good report
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “a good testimony,” the phrase refers to the witness others bear about a person’s character. The Seven of Acts 6 were to be men “of honest report,” and Cornelius was well spoken of among the Jews. Paul extends that expectation to the overseer’s standing among unbelievers.

wordNotes.term: παγίδα τοῦ διαβόλου (pagida tou diabolou) — the snare of the devil
wordNotes.explanation: A pagis is a trap or noose for catching animals. Paul uses the image for the devil’s schemes that capture people unawares, and also for the desire for riches that becomes a snare. Escape comes through God-given repentance and recovery of a sober mind.

verses.bibleText: Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Likewise” introduces a second group, the deacons. The Greek word means servant or minister, and Paul often uses it broadly of himself and his co-workers. Here, as in Philippians 1:1, it stands beside the overseers and names a recognized office. Acts 6, where seven men were chosen to administer the daily distribution so that the apostles could give themselves to prayer and the word, supplies a pattern of practical service entrusted to men of proven character, even though the Seven are not given the title there.

The first requirement is “grave”: worthy of respect, serious in bearing. “Not doubletongued” means not saying one thing to one person and something different to another. Deacons who moved among homes would hear a great deal. A man who reshapes his words to please each listener spreads confusion and mistrust, and he soon becomes a carrier of tales. Integrity of speech is required of anyone trusted with people’s confidences.

“Not given to much wine” and “not greedy of filthy lucre” repeat concerns raised for the overseers, in slightly stronger terms. Paul’s wording targets indulgence; it is not framed as a measured allowance, and Scripture’s wider counsel against strong drink and its call to temperance apply to every servant of the church (Proverbs 23:31-32). If deacons handled the church’s gifts for the poor, as the Seven did, greed for shameful gain would be a special temptation. Money given in trust for widows and the needy must pass through clean hands.

wordNotes.explanation: The word means servant, attendant, or minister. In many passages it describes any servant of Christ, including Paul and Timothy. In this chapter, set alongside the overseer and given its own qualifications, it has become the title of an office devoted to practical service in the congregation.

Literally “double-worded,” the term describes someone who gives conflicting accounts to different people or says one thing while meaning another. It strikes at the root of trust. Scripture elsewhere condemns the double heart and the flattering lip that go with such speech.

verses.bibleText: Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The deacon’s qualifications now move from conduct to conviction. He must hold “the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience.” In Paul’s usage a mystery is a truth once hidden and now made known by God—the purpose of salvation disclosed in Christ (Romans 16:25-26; Colossians 1:26-27). “The faith” here is the body of Christian teaching. Verse 16 will name the content of this mystery: Christ himself.

Deacons are not required to be “apt to teach” as overseers are, but they must understand and hold fast what the church believes. Practical service is never detached from doctrine. A deacon who visits the sick or distributes aid will be asked the reason for his hope, and he must know and believe it.

The phrase “in a pure conscience” binds belief to life. Paul opened the letter by describing love that flows “out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience” (1:5), and he warned that some had thrust conscience aside and made shipwreck of the faith (1:19). The false teachers would hold their doctrines with consciences seared as with a hot iron (4:2). Truth held while conscience is violated will not be held for long. The deacon must be a man whose inner life agrees with the faith he professes.

wordNotes.term: τὸ μυστήριον τῆς πίστεως (to mystērion tēs pisteōs) — the mystery of the faith
wordNotes.explanation: In Paul a mystērion is a divine purpose formerly hidden and now revealed to all through the gospel, not an esoteric secret for initiates. Joined with “the faith,” it refers to the revealed content of Christian belief. The phrase anticipates “the mystery of godliness” in verse 16, where that content is shown to be Christ.

verses.bibleText: And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And let these also first be proved” means that deacons, like overseers, are to be examined before they serve. The verb was used for testing metals and for approving a candidate after scrutiny. Paul describes no formal procedure, but 5:22 warns against laying hands on anyone hastily, and the letter itself makes the qualifications public. A congregation aware of these standards can observe a man’s life over time and judge his fitness.

Only then may they “use the office of a deacon,” serving “being found blameless.” The word for blameless differs from the one in verse 2, but the idea is close: no charge can stand against them. Office is not a remedy for spiritual weakness. Appointing a careless member in the hope that responsibility will stir him to zeal reverses Paul’s order. Testing comes first, then service.

The principle reaches every ministry. Those entrusted with any work in the church should be known, observed, and found faithful. Such care protects the congregation, and it also protects the servant from burdens he is not yet ready to bear.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to test with a view to approval, as metal is assayed to show its worth. Paul uses it for examining one’s own work and for proving what is good. Here the testing is meant to confirm fitness, not to look for grounds of rejection.

The adjective means unaccused, free from any charge that could be brought in court. It is the word Paul uses of the elders in Titus and of believers presented without charge before Christ. The deacon’s record must withstand honest examination.

verses.bibleText: Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul pauses within the deacon section to address women. The Greek word can mean either “women” or “wives,” and the KJV chose “their wives,” supplying “their,” which is not in the text. Two main readings carry real weight. Some take these to be the wives of deacons, who would share in their husbands’ visitation and care; the verse sits between two statements about deacons, and the next verse turns to their marriages. Others take them to be women who served in a diaconal capacity. “Even so” introduces them exactly as “likewise” introduced deacons after overseers in verse 8, and the four qualities listed mirror those required of deacons. Phoebe is called a “servant”—the same word as deacon—of the church at Cenchrea, and early Christian sources mention women who served in this way.

Certainty is not possible, and the text’s own reserve should be respected. What is clear is that women were involved in the church’s ministry of service and that their character mattered to the apostle. In a society where men could not easily visit women in secluded households, women who could carry care, instruction, and aid into those homes were invaluable. Whether as deacons’ wives or as servants in their own right, they were held to a standard matching that of the deacons.

They must be “grave,” worthy of respect, like the deacons of verse 8. They must not be “slanderers”; the word is the same one used elsewhere for “the devil,” the accuser. Gossip that wounds and divides does the adversary’s work. They must be “sober,” clear-minded and temperate, and “faithful in all things,” fully reliable in whatever is placed in their hands, whether confidences, goods for the poor, or the welfare of the sick.

The list answers dangers already visible at Ephesus, where some younger widows were becoming “tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not” (5:13). Paul’s answer was to make sure that women who served did so with dignity, discretion, and trustworthy hands, not to shut them out of the church’s service.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun means “women” and, in a suitable context, “wives.” Both senses occur in this letter: “women” in 2:9-12 and “wife” in 3:2 and 3:12. Because no possessive is present and the women are introduced with “likewise,” the reference may be to women serving as deacons; the setting between statements about deacons also allows the sense “their wives.”

Diabolos means slanderer or false accuser and, with the article, is the regular title of the devil. Applied to people, it describes those who spread damaging talk. Paul lists slanderers among the marks of the last days and warns older women in Crete against the same fault.

verses.bibleText: Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul returns to the deacons themselves. They too must be “the husbands of one wife,” faithful in marriage, and they must lead their children and households well. The requirements match those for overseers in verses 2 and 4, word for word in places. The home is the proving ground for every officer of the church, whether he teaches or serves.

One difference is instructive. Paul does not repeat the reasoning of verse 5, which tied management of a household to care for the church of God. Deacons are not given oversight of the congregation. The household standard still applies, because a deacon’s service carries him into many homes and his own must commend his work. Faith that fails at home will not persuade elsewhere.

These verses also honor domestic life. Against teachers who would soon forbid marriage (4:3), Paul presents a faithful marriage and a well-ordered family as qualifications for service. The home is itself a place of discipleship.

wordNotes.explanation: The adverb “well” or “commendably” runs through Paul’s instructions for officers: overseers rule their homes well, deacons do the same, elders who rule well deserve double honor, and those who serve well gain a good standing. The repetition stresses quality of service rather than the mere holding of a position.

verses.bibleText: For they that have used the office of a deacon well purchase to themselves a good degree, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The section on deacons closes with encouragement, just as the section on overseers opened with one. “They that have used the office of a deacon well” refers to those who have served faithfully. Two results follow: “a good degree” and “great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.”

“Degree” translates a word meaning a step or standing. Some have taken it as promotion to higher office, but that would turn the deacon’s work into a stepping-stone and undercut the honor Paul gives it. More likely it refers to good standing—esteem and influence within the congregation earned by trustworthy service, and perhaps standing before God as well. Paul does not teach that faithful service merits salvation or a higher rank in eternity; salvation remains by grace through faith, and good works are its fruit (Ephesians 2:8-10). Yet faithfulness bears results. The servant becomes trusted, and his word carries weight.

“Great boldness” is confident freedom of speech and approach. The same word describes believers’ access to God through Christ and the apostles’ fearless witness before the council (Acts 4:13, 29). Those who have served faithfully grow in confidence, both before people as witnesses and before God in prayer. Two of the Seven in Acts illustrate the point: Stephen spoke with wisdom his opponents could not resist, and Philip preached Christ in Samaria and to the Ethiopian official.

That confidence is “in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.” It rests on the One he trusts, not on the deacon’s own record. Faithful service draws a believer into fuller reliance on Christ, and the servant grows bolder as he learns that the Lord stands with him.

wordNotes.term: βαθμὸν … καλόν (bathmon … kalon) — a good degree
wordNotes.explanation: Bathmos, found only here in the New Testament, means a step or threshold and figuratively a standing or position. Since the deacon’s office is itself called good, the phrase is best read as honorable standing gained through faithful service, not promotion to another office. Jesus’ parable of the faithful servant offers a similar picture of trust widened through faithfulness.

The word denotes openness and confidence, originally the citizen’s freedom to speak in public assembly. In the New Testament it describes courageous witness before people and confident access to God through Christ. Both senses suit those who have served well.

verses.bibleText: These things write I unto thee, hoping to come unto thee shortly:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul steps back from the lists to explain why he writes. “These things write I unto thee” refers at least to the instructions just given and probably to the letter as a whole. He hopes to come to Timothy soon. The letter is no substitute for his presence, but it carries his authority until he arrives.

Paul’s plans were often overtaken by events. He had left Timothy at Ephesus while he went on into Macedonia (1:3), and whether he ever returned there is unknown. Later he wrote again from prison, urging Timothy to come to him before winter. He had learned to hold every plan under the condition “if the Lord will.”

A written charge also strengthened Timothy’s position. Read before the congregation, it gave him the apostle’s open support for decisions about leaders and teaching that some would resist. The church still receives Paul’s counsel in this written form, an apostolic word that has outlasted his journeys.

wordNotes.explanation: The phrase means soon or without long delay. It expresses Paul’s intention, not a fixed schedule; the next verse immediately allows that he may be delayed. He uses similar language of sending Timothy to Philippi and of visiting Corinth “if the Lord will.”

verses.bibleText: But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But if I tarry long” allows for delay. Paul writes “that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God.” The KJV supplies “thou,” but the Greek has no expressed subject; it may mean how Timothy himself should act, or how people in general ought to conduct themselves in God’s household. Both are true, since the letter instructs Timothy so that he can order the whole congregation. The verb refers to one’s entire way of life, not merely behavior during worship.

“The house of God” means God’s household, the family he has gathered. The believers at Ephesus owned no church buildings; they met in homes. Yet the Lord lived among them. The earlier picture of a man managing his household (3:4-5) now widens to God as head of the house, with his people as members of his family (Ephesians 2:19). The house is further named “the church of the living God,” a pointed description in a city devoted to Artemis, whose temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world. The living God dwells in a living temple made of people.

The church is “the pillar and ground of the truth.” A pillar holds up and displays; the second word, found only here in the New Testament, refers to a foundation, support, or buttress. The phrase does not make the church the source of truth or set it above Scripture. Truth comes from God and is revealed in his Word, and the church itself rests on that foundation (Ephesians 2:20). Its calling is to uphold the truth, keep it standing in the world, and lift it where others can see it. A congregation does this through faithful teaching and through lives that agree with what it teaches.

When believers abandon the truth or live in contradiction to it, the pillar cracks, and onlookers conclude that the truth itself is weak. When they hold it faithfully and reflect God’s character, they become witnesses to the power of his grace. That is why the qualifications of verses 1-13 matter so much. Conduct in God’s household is never a minor concern.

wordNotes.term: οἴκῳ θεοῦ (oikō theou) — the house of God
wordNotes.explanation: Oikos can mean a building or a household. Here it refers to God’s family, the people among whom he dwells. The same word was used of the overseer’s own house in verses 4-5, so the church is pictured as a household with God as its head and Father.

wordNotes.term: στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα (stylos kai hedraiōma) — pillar and ground
wordNotes.explanation: Stylos is a column, used of leaders who were “pillars” at Jerusalem and of the overcomer made a pillar in God’s temple. Hedraiōma, which appears only here in the New Testament, means a support or foundation, related to a word for steadfast. Together they picture the church as the structure that bears up and holds aloft the truth God has revealed.

verses.bibleText: And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Without controversy” means by common confession, beyond dispute. What follows is what every believer acknowledges: “great is the mystery of godliness.” Godliness here is the true religion that the false teachers distorted into a means of gain (6:5), and its mystery is the secret God has now made known. Paul does not answer with a principle or a program. He answers with a person. The six balanced lines that follow are widely recognized as an early Christian hymn or confession used in worship.

The KJV reads “God was manifest in the flesh,” following later manuscripts. The oldest Greek manuscripts read “who” or “he who was manifest.” In the capital script of early copies, the customary abbreviation for “God” differs from the word “who” by two small strokes, so a copyist could easily read one as the other. The earlier reading is probably original, and its subject is plainly Christ. One who “was manifest in the flesh” existed before taking flesh, so the line affirms both his preexistence and his real humanity. The deity of Christ stands firmly on many other texts (John 1:1, 14; Colossians 2:9; Titus 2:13) and does not depend on a single disputed word here.

The hymn moves in three pairs, each joining earth and heaven. “Manifest in the flesh” celebrates the incarnation: the Son became truly human (2:5). “Justified in the Spirit” means vindicated. The One condemned and crucified by men was declared righteous and shown to be the Son of God by the Spirit’s power in his resurrection (Romans 1:4). “Seen of angels” recalls the heavenly witnesses of his resurrection and ascension, beings who long to look into the gospel (1 Peter 1:12). “Preached unto the Gentiles” and “believed on in the world” trace the message’s spread and its reception by faith. “Received up into glory” points to the ascension, when Christ was taken up and seated at the right hand of God.

The hymn does not name the cross, yet it assumes it: vindication implies a verdict reversed, and exaltation implies a prior humiliation. The final line also directs attention to Christ’s present work. Ascended into glory, he now ministers for his people as High Priest in the heavenly sanctuary (Hebrews 8:1-2), and he will appear a second time, visibly and in glory, for those who wait for him (Hebrews 9:24, 28).

This confession is the foundation beneath chapters 2 and 3. The church’s order, its leaders’ character, and its members’ conduct all flow from the Christ it confesses. Godliness is first a mystery revealed and only then a life lived. The false teachers offered myths and endless genealogies; the household of God holds aloft a living Lord.

wordNotes.term: ὃς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκί (hos ephanerōthē en sarki) — God was manifest in the flesh
wordNotes.explanation: The earliest manuscripts read hos, “who,” where later copies read theos, “God”; in early capital script the two looked very similar. Either way the subject is Christ. The verb means to be made visible or revealed, implying that the One revealed already existed. Other New Testament writers use the same verb for the Son’s appearing in human life.

wordNotes.term: ἐδικαιώθη ἐν πνεύματι (edikaiōthē en pneumati) — justified in the Spirit
wordNotes.explanation: Here the verb means vindicated or shown to be in the right, not pardoned. Christ, rejected and condemned on earth, was publicly vindicated by the Spirit when God raised him from the dead and declared him to be his Son with power. The line answers the verdict of the cross with the verdict of the resurrection.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: Why might Scripture give so much more attention to a leader’s character than to his abilities?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God entrusts his household to servants whose tested character, faithful homes, and sound teaching agree with the Christ the church confesses.
discussionQuestions: Why does Paul treat a man’s household as evidence of his fitness to care for the church?
What danger does Paul see in appointing a recent convert, and how does pride connect with the devil’s fall?
How should a congregation “prove” those it appoints to serve?
In what sense is the church “the pillar and ground of the truth” without becoming the source of truth?
How should the confession of 3:16 shape the conduct of leaders and members alike?
commonMisunderstandings: “The husband of one wife” does not require every leader to be married or forbid a widower to remarry; it demands a life of marital faithfulness.
Blamelessness is not sinless perfection; it describes a settled pattern of life that gives no just ground for accusation.
The church upholds and displays the truth, but it does not create the truth or stand above God’s revealed Word.
Serving well brings good standing and confidence in the faith; it does not earn salvation or rank in eternity.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep character and doctrine together: the qualifications of 3:1-13 and the confession of 3:16 belong to one household whose conduct must agree with the truth it holds.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Whatever place you hold in God’s household, let the Christ who was manifest in the flesh govern your home, your speech, and your service.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: The mystery of godliness is a person: Christ, manifest in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, proclaimed and believed, and received up into glory.
flow: True godliness is not invented by human effort; God has revealed it in Christ.
The eternal Son took real human flesh and lived among us.
Rejected and crucified by men, he was vindicated when the Spirit raised him from the dead.
He is proclaimed among the nations and received by faith throughout the world.
Ascended into glory, he ministers for his people now, and the church lives as his household until he appears.
simpleIllustrations: A pillar does not create the roof it bears; it holds the roof up where people can see it and find shelter beneath it.
A family name is honored or shamed by how its members live among their neighbors.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you believe on the Christ who came in the flesh and now reigns in glory, and take your place in the household that lives by his truth?
cautions: Do not present leadership qualifications as a ladder by which anyone earns salvation.
Do not rest the deity of Christ on the disputed reading in 3:16 alone; many plain texts teach it.
Do not shame those whose homes carry painful histories; the passage concerns fitness for office, not a person’s worth before God.

reflectionQuestions: Do I desire responsibility in God’s work for the sake of the work or for the recognition it brings?
What would people who know me outside the church say about my honesty and conduct?
How faithfully am I leading or serving within my own household?
Where has pride begun to cloud my judgment?
How does the confession of Christ in 3:16 change the way I conduct myself in God’s house?
